name: Risk compensation
statement: Making an activity safer can lead people to behave more riskily, so part or all of the intended safety gain is handed back through changed behaviour.
meaning: The idea comes in two strengths, and they are routinely treated as one. The weak version says a safety measure changes behaviour to some degree, so the benefit measured in the field is smaller than the benefit measured on a test rig. Almost nobody disputes that this can happen. The strong version says the offset is complete: people hold a fixed target level of risk, and any measure that lowers risk is met by behaviour that restores it. Gerald Wilde called the strong version risk homeostasis and wrote in 1982 that the accident rate is ultimately dependent on one factor only, the target level of risk in the population concerned. The strong version has a policy consequence the weak one does not, because it implies that engineering and regulation cannot work at all, and only changing what people want can. Which version is being defended is the first thing to establish in any argument about this.

origin.note: Peltzman's paper is about American car safety regulation and never uses the phrase now attached to it. The names came later from other people: the Peltzman effect for his result, and risk homeostasis from Gerald Wilde's 1982 paper in Risk Analysis, which turned it into a general theory of behaviour.

evidence: Peltzman's abstract sets out the claim in four sentences. Engineering studies implied annual highway deaths would be 20 per cent higher without the mandated safety devices. That literature ignored non-regulatory demand for safety and drivers' response to the devices. His analysis of the fatality rate found these offsets virtually complete, so regulation had not reduced highway deaths. Time-series data, though not cross-section data, implied some saving of car occupants' lives at the cost of more pedestrian deaths and more non-fatal crashes. The last sentence is the mechanism: drivers protected inside the car impose the risk on people outside it.

replication.headline: Tested properly, the offset is usually small or absent, but it is not absent everywhere, and the domains have to be judged separately.
replication.detail: Car safety regulation. Leon Robertson answered Peltzman in the Journal of Economic Issues in 1977, and Barry Pless's 2016 review reports that this reanalysis of Peltzman's own data found numerous errors. Robertson then used 236,000 vehicles in fatal American crashes from 1975 to 1978 and found the federal standards cut occupant deaths per 100 million miles travelled and also cut fatal collisions with pedestrians, motorcyclists and cyclists, which is the opposite of Peltzman's displacement claim. He put the total at about 37,000 fewer deaths over those four years. Seat belts. Alma Cohen and Liran Einav built a panel of all 50 states and the District of Columbia for 1983 to 1997 and instrumented belt usage with the laws themselves. A one-point rise in usage saved 136 lives, and the effect on non-occupant deaths, the group that can only be harmed by careless driving, was a coefficient of -0.042 with a standard error of 0.121 on 556 observations. They concluded there is no strong support for the Peltzman effect. Jinpeng Lv and colleagues went back to the same 1983 to 1997 panel in 2015 and did find Peltzman effects on non-occupant fatalities, mainly where primary enforcement arrived directly, and found the effects faded over time. Bicycle helmets. Mohsen Esmaeilikia and colleagues screened 145 articles and included 23. Eighteen found no evidence that helmet use went with riskier behaviour, three were mixed, and the two supportive studies came from a single laboratory. Ross Phillips, Aslak Fyhri and Fridulv Sagberg had 35 cyclists ride 0.4 km downhill with and without a helmet: routine helmet users went slower and reported more risk when the helmet was removed, while cyclists unused to helmets showed no change on any measure. Ski helmets. Michael Scott and colleagues observed and interviewed 1,779 adults at 34 resorts and found helmet wearers reported slower speeds (OR 0.64) and less self-challenge (OR 0.76) than non-wearers, the reverse of compensation. HIV prophylaxis. The PROUD trial randomised 544 men in England to immediate or deferred pre-exposure prophylaxis and detected no difference between the groups in sexually transmitted infections, including rectal gonorrhoea and chlamydia, despite a suggestion of risk compensation among some recipients. Michael Traeger's meta-analysis of 16 observational studies and one open-label trial found rectal chlamydia raised (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.19 to 2.13) and any STI diagnosis at OR 1.24 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.54), with most studies reporting more condomless sex. Motor racing. Russell Sobel and Todd Nesbit examined NASCAR, where the outcome data are individual rather than aggregate, and report that their results strongly support offsetting behaviour.

study.cite: Cohen, A., & Einav, L. (2003). The effects of mandatory seat belt laws on driving behavior and traffic fatalities. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 85(4), 828-843.

limits: No systematic review of risk compensation across domains was located. Searches of PubMed, Crossref, OpenAlex and the open web turned up Esmaeilikia's 2019 review, which covers cycling only, and Barry Pless's 2016 piece in Safety, which states in its own text that it makes no pretence of being systematic. So the domain-by-domain picture above is assembled here rather than read off a single source, and the domains are not weighted against each other. The best-tested cases are also the ones with the most political attention, which is not a random sample. Cohen and Einav's null on non-occupant deaths and Lv's positive finding come from the same panel of years and states, so the disagreement is about specification rather than data. The PROUD trial ran for a year in one country, and STI screening intensity rises when people enter a prophylaxis programme, which inflates measured infection rates independently of behaviour. Wilde's strong version is close to untestable as stated, because any measured offset short of complete can be attributed to the target level of risk having shifted.
misreadings: Ian Walker's 2007 study, in which drivers passed closer to a helmeted cyclist, is not a risk compensation finding. It measures the behaviour of other people towards someone wearing safety equipment, not the wearer's own behaviour, and Walker attributed it to drivers judging rider competence from appearance. Its history is also usually told backwards. Jake Olivier and Scott Walter reanalysed Walker's 2,355 passing events in 2013, split them at one metre, and found helmet wearing unrelated to close passing (adjusted OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.68, p = 0.54), while their own continuous model still gave a 5.8 cm reduction. Walker and Dorothy Robinson replied in 2019 that moving the one-metre cut-off slightly reverses the reanalysis, and their fresh analysis found the whole distribution shifted just over a fifth of a standard deviation closer. Walker was not an author of the reanalysis, and the reanalysis did not settle the question. The other frequent error is treating the Peltzman effect as established because it is famous. Peltzman claimed a complete offset in one country's road fatality statistics in 1975, and the strongest later support comes from stock car racing rather than public roads. Laboratory demonstrations do not stand in for the field either: Tim Gamble and Walker's 2016 finding that an unmentioned helmet raised risk taking on computer tasks drew a published comment in the same journal titled "Bicycle Helmets and the Experimenter Effect".
